newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bangladesh says halting Burmese expulsions - UNHCR.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh says halting Burmese expulsions - UNHCR.

text.p: Bangladesh officials have announced that they are halting the forced repatriation of thousands of Burmese Moslems, the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Wednesday.

UNHCR spokeswoman Pam O'Toole said the announcement was made in camps where about 21,000 refugees live southeast Bangladesh and followed talks between UNHCR representatives and Bangladesh officials in the capital Dhaka.
"We welcome this move and look forward to seeing that expulsions that had apparently been planned for tomorrow (Thursday) have been cancelled," she told Reuters.
"We will continue talks to ensure that those of the refugees who want to stay are not forced back."
UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner Sergio Vieira de Mello earlier sent a letter of protest over the expulsions to Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad, saying they violated international law.
The repatriations sparked clashes between riot police and refugees in camps just inside Bangladesh's southeastern border in which several people were injured.

De Mello's letter said: "We have also received reports of maltreatment of refugees during the preparation for their return, including physical abuse, the separation of at least 67 minors from their mothers and the return of individuals who are ill or handicapped and therefore unfit for repatriation without medical supervision."
About 21,000 of the Rohinga refugees are left in Bangladesh out of nearly 250,000 who fled across the border in the early 1990s.

Many said they were escaping persecution by Burma's military rulers. The Bangladesh government argues that they are economic migrants who place a heavy burden on the economy of one of the world's least-developed countries.

Most of the original refugees have returned under voluntary repatriation programmes supervised by the UNHCR. But the refugee agency says that, aside from those still left behind, more are now crossing over from Burma.
De Mello urged the government to halt forced repatriations and allow the agency to interview those returning to ensure they were going back of their own free will.

"In the absence of such arrangements," he said, "the UNHCR would no longer be in a position to associate itself with the repatriation operation" under which most of the earlier refugees returned voluntarily.

The UNHCR said tension had been rising in refugee camps amid reports of further expulsions on Thursday. In one camp, refugees had refused their food rations for the past four days and locked themselves in their huts.

Some said they would prefer to starve rather than return to Burma, the agency said. In another camp, it said, several hundred Rohingas were involved earlier on Wednesday in a tense stand-off with police.
